text: Zhang Meili starts a school in the dry country of northwest China, and everything that follows comes out of that one stubborn act. Xia Yu arrives from Beijing to help: cheerful, urban, certain about what children need. The two are not set against each other in the way the setup promises; what Yang Yazhou wants is the slower business of each woman learning the other's terms. A second, looser register runs alongside that one — a husband who comes out from the city to argue his wife home, a courtship with the local projectionist conducted with more secrecy than a small place can hold. A hundred and three minutes, built as one incident handing off to the next rather than as a single climb, which suits a story about work that has to be started again every morning.

Mountains decide the shape of a battle before any commander does, and a war film set in the Tai Hang range inherits that problem whether it wants it or not. Lian Wei puts Zhu De and the Eighth Route Army into those slopes against the Japanese invasion, which commits the film to two jobs that pull against each other: terrain, supply, the physical cost of moving men uphill, and then the single named commander the frame keeps returning to. A hundred and seventeen minutes leaves room to fail at either. It helps that the outcome of the war is settled for everyone watching. Suspense is not where the film spends itself, and what it buys instead is the conduct of the fighting: where a line holds, what holding it costs, who is standing behind whom when the order goes out.

A boat on a river, six years of prison behind one of the passengers, and two officers obliged to sit with him the whole way. Qiu Shi is a poet under transfer; the transfer is the plot and the deck is the set. Wu Yonggang keeps other travellers coming aboard, each carrying some recent damage, and the confinement does the work an interrogation would do in a coarser film: people who cannot speak plainly have to be read sideways. Eighty-six minutes, one boat, a country moving past the rail. It was made in 1980 about the last stretch of the Cultural Revolution, which means the first audiences could still count the months since, and knew exactly which silences on that deck were being performed.

Two documents govern this film: a teaching certificate she does not have, and the college entrance examination her students will sit. The certificate would make her a government employee, with the pay and the way out that implies. The examination is the only door out of a poor rural district for the children in front of her, and their whole preparation for it is one unqualified woman who did not choose the job. He Qun sets those papers at opposite ends of ninety minutes and refuses to let either discredit the other; the ambition and the obligation turn out to be the same day's work, done in the same room. The economy of the place stays visible throughout — an examination written elsewhere, by people who will never see this classroom, deciding which of these children gets another kind of life.

An eye surgeon's heart gives out, and the film turns around to look at the years that brought her there. The accounting she makes from the bed is the ordinary kind, which is why it is hard: she was not much of a wife, not much of a mother, and she took a great many people out of blindness, and neither column cancels the other. Wang Qimin lets both stand unreconciled for ninety-eight minutes. The 1982 date does quiet work. A woman's professional life is set directly against her household, and nobody in the film is granted the authority to say which was owed the debt. The structure helps: collapse first, then the career recovered in pieces, so that every scene of competence arrives already shadowed by what it cost at home.

A sixteen-year-old corrects her teacher in front of the class, and is right, and that is the trouble. An-ran rebels at nothing in particular; she will simply not agree with something false because an adult said it, and Lu Xiaoya treats that refusal as a whole subject rather than a stage to be grown out of. The scale stays small — a school, a household, the daily calculation of when agreement is worth its price — and the smallness is the argument. Ninety-seven minutes, 1985, and no villain on offer: the adults around her are people who learned earlier than she did what going along costs and what it saves, and who now have to watch someone decline the arrangement out loud, in a room where everyone can see it happen.

A mansion in the old French concession, carved into flats for several families, and one of those families used to own all of it. Peng Xiaolian follows them through and past that conversion: money before, subdivision during the Cultural Revolution, and whatever the arrangement has become now that everyone is older. The upheaval is the hinge rather than the subject. What the hundred minutes are actually about is the long afterward, and what a family says at the table when the house it grew up in is still standing and no longer theirs in the way it was. Shanghai supplies the rest. A city whose buildings openly record who used to live where is a hard place to forget in, and the film works that seam, an address meaning one thing on a document and another in the corridor.

In the spring of 1949 an army starts moving toward the Yangtze, and the film gives itself a hundred and sixty-three minutes to get across it. Xiao Guiyun's subject is a campaign whose outcome nobody in the audience needs explained, which changes the job entirely: not what happens, but who says what to whom during the weeks it takes to happen. The scale is the state's: armies on one hand, and on the other a few rooms where Mao Zedong and the people around Chiang Kai-Shek read telegrams and decide. Its opening movement is the crossing itself and the fall of Nanjing in April. China sent the picture out as its submission to the Academy Awards, an odd errand for a work that assumes a viewer who already knows every name on screen and cares which of them is standing where.

Thirty-two years on a small island at the border, two people, and a job whose content is mostly the fact of still being there. Wang Jicai and his wife Shihua kept Kashan; Chen Li has a hundred and twenty-five minutes to render three decades of a duty made out of repetition. That compression is the film's real problem, and a productive one. A story with no natural episodes has to invent its own units, so weather, seasons and the anniversaries that pass on a rock become the structure it does not otherwise have. The marriage carries the rest. Not a topic the film discusses, but the arrangement that makes the posting survivable: two people who turned a duty roster into a household, and then kept that household running long enough for it to become the point.

Money arrives in a Shaanxi village, and people who had made no plans to be rearranged are rearranged. Yan Xueshu set his film in the north of the province in 1985 and watched the country's economic change reach a place remote enough to have missed several earlier ones. Nothing in the treatment is schematic. Change of that kind shows up at village scale as ordinary domestic argument: who is willing to try the new thing, who is not, and how quickly that difference stops being about money and starts being about marriages, neighbours, who still speaks to whom. A hundred minutes, and the frame never leaves the village. The film assumes a village is subject enough and never goes looking for a larger one.

The workers at the textile mill are in uproar, and the mayor who has to answer them used to run that mill himself. Li Gaocheng appointed the managers now accused of taking money meant for the plant, which is the trap Yu Benzheng builds the film inside: every document that damns them also says something about the judgement of the man who chose them. Two hours and forty minutes is a great deal of screen time for accounts and personnel, and the length is the method. What it wants is the slowness of finding out, the way certainty about the people he vouched for comes apart in increments rather than in a single scene. The mill is the city's employment, so nothing stays abstract for long. What has gone missing is wages, and the people owed them are outside in the street.

In this village the law is a man, and the man is not a villain, which is the difficulty the film begins with. The chief settles what needs settling by a code he carries in his own head, and it has worked well enough that nobody local calls it anything but order, until someone goes over his head and the state arrives with questions. Fan Yuan is not exposing a tyrant. He is watching two systems of justice, each of which has kept this place upright, forced into the same room, where everyone involved can give a reasonable account of himself. A hundred and thirteen minutes at village scale, the camera close to people who have known each other their whole lives and are now required to say, on the record, what they have seen.
